params.text:
Recording and writing it up

A report is only useful if it is clear, honest and factual. Whether you use a paper accident book, an incident form or a digital system, the same principles apply: record what actually happened in plain, objective language.

  • Record factually — write what you saw, heard and did, in the order it happened, using the person’s own words in quotation marks where you can. Keep out opinions, guesswork and blame.
  • Be accurate — include who, what, when, where and any witnesses, along with the exact time, the location, who was present and any injuries or effects you noticed.
  • Report promptly — while the details are fresh, ideally before the end of your shift.
  • Sign and date the record so it is clear who completed it and when.

Stick to facts, not assumptions. ‘I found Mr Ali sitting on the floor beside his bed’ is a fact; ‘Mr Ali fell because he was being careless’ is an assumption you did not witness. Avoid labels and avoid blaming anyone; if you genuinely must record an opinion, make it clear that is what it is. Describe events plainly, for example: “Mrs A was found sitting on the floor beside her bed at 14:10. She said she felt dizzy. No visible injury. First aider called, GP informed.”

A body map — an outline of the body on which you mark the site, size and appearance of any injury — helps you describe bruises or wounds precisely without handling the person unnecessarily. Do not leave gaps or use correction fluid; if you make a mistake, cross it out with a single line, initial it, and write the correction alongside. Sign and date the report, because it is a legal record that may later be read by managers, the CQC, families or a court.

params.textField: Always record what happened *factually*, sticking to the facts and not to opinions about blame. Make sure your account is *accurate*, including who, what, when and where. Complete the report *promptly*, before details are forgotten. Finally, *sign* and date the entry so it is clear who wrote it, and keep the information *confidential*, sharing it only with those who need it.

Use a *body* map to show exactly where an injury is, and never use correction *fluid* to hide a mistake. Finally, *sign* the report, because it is a legal record.
